_about: Real numbers for the life flight traits (traits/life.js): the suit's oxygen, the ship's spare oxygen in kilograms per tank, the gas each trip outside vents, CO2 scrubbing, water, radiation shielding. Every number names a source id from `sources`; 'estimate' marks a defensible guess where no public figure was found. GAME SCALING (stated, not hidden): the game flies one astronaut; the game shows the suit's 7.3 h of walking on one fill as 300 s (about 87 times faster); the planned stores of the cabin's life-support loop for the 259-day cruise (about 0.9 t of water, 218 kg of breathing oxygen and 0.4 t of LiOH for an open loop) are carried by the capsule as planned stores: they add no mass in the game and are NOT charged to the spare tanks. The spare tanks pay for the stay on Mars: each trip outside costs the suit's fill, the cabin air vented through the hatch or the airlock, and the cabin breathing for the rest of that sol (0.84 kg/day × 17.4 h; none with the regenerative loop, whose oxygen generator makes it from water). A sea-level cabin also loses its nitrogen with each emptying (0.91 kg/m³), drawn from a nitrogen allowance; when that runs out the cabin is refilled with pure oxygen at 5 psi instead (Apollo style), which costs more oxygen. The water recycler has no felt effect yet: the planned stores cover the water either way, and the hangar analysis shows how much water it saved. What the player's choices change: the spare oxygen for walks outside, what each trip outside costs, backups for the scrubber, the radiation shielding.

body._src: bvad, metabolicO2; water: 2.5 kg drinking + 0.5 kg food preparation (bvad), hygiene water left out (estimate)

mixed._src: ISS and Soyuz cabin air; prebreathe: ISS protocols of 2 to 4 h before a 29.6 kPa suit (prebreathe)

pure_o2._src: Mercury, Gemini, Apollo cabins at 5 psi of oxygen: no nitrogen in the blood, so no prebreathe (prebreathe)

pad_mix._src: Apollo CM from Apollo 7: 60/40 on the pad, bled to pure oxygen at 5 psi after launch (prebreathe)

cabins._about: Free (pressurised) volume of each crew cabin in m³. With no airlock, the crew empties the whole cabin to go outside (Gemini, Apollo) and refills it from the spare oxygen afterwards.

starship_nose._src: capsules; the built-in airlock is an estimate from the HLS design

airlocks._about: Volume of an airlock part in m³: only this volume is emptied for each trip outside.

volga_airlock._src: volga (2.5 m long, 1.0 m wide inside: π·0.5²·2.5)

soyuz_orbital_module._src: estimate (Soyuz 4/5 used it as the airlock in 1969)

shenzhou_orbital_module._src: estimate (Shenzhou 7 used it as the airlock in 2008)

steel_hp.name: steel high-pressure cylinder
steel_hp._src: cylinder; the last gas below the suit's 62 bar cannot flow into the suit (emuO2)

cryo.name: cryogenic supercritical tank
cryo._src: apolloTank (delivers at 900 psi until nearly empty; residual: estimate)

tanks._about: Spare oxygen per part: kg of O2 at launch, storage pressure (bar), share of the contents lost per day (valve seep or boil-off), and how many separate tanks (each with its own valve).

o2_bottle._src: cylinder (one 50 L steel cylinder at 150 bar: about 10.4 kg; the 41 % below the suit's 62 bar cannot fill the suit, so about 6.1 kg usable); leak: valve seat at the ISO 10297 limit of 6 cm³/h, about 0.2 g/day (estimate)

o2_tank_l._src: nors (a NORS-class composite-overwrapped tank: 36.3 kg at 6000 psi; only 15 % is below the suit's 62 bar, so about 30.9 kg usable); one valve: about 0.2 g/day (estimate)

capsule_l._src: estimate (a crew module's own high-pressure O₂ tank)

vostok_instrument_module._src: estimate (Vostok carried its oxygen and nitrogen in spherical bottles around the instrument module)

gemini_adapter._src: estimate (Gemini's primary oxygen was supercritical in the adapter, sized for 14 days); boil-off: estimate (ground LOX dewars lose 1–2 %/day)

apollo_sm._src: apolloTank (two tanks of 320 lb of supercritical oxygen at 865–935 psi); boil-off: estimate

orion_esm._src: esm (three oxygen tanks, 90 kg in all); pressure: estimate

progress_cargo_module._src: estimate (Progress delivers oxygen and air in high-pressure tanks)

cygnus_pcm._src: nors (one NORS recharge tank as cargo: 36.3 kg of O₂ at 6000 psi)

atv_icc._src: atv (up to 100 kg of oxygen, nitrogen and air; the oxygen share is an estimate)

tanks.apollo_sm_note: Apollo's fuel cells also drew on these tanks; the game leaves the fuel cells' share out (estimate)

fallbackTank._src: any other part with spare O₂ counts as one 50 L bottle per spareO2Tanks (estimate)

nitrogen._src: esm (Orion's service module carries one 30 kg nitrogen tank; taken as every sea-level cabin's nitrogen for refilling it on Mars: estimate)

mars._src: a Mars sol is 24 h 39.6 min; the cabin breathing between walks is 0.84 kg/day × (sol − suit hours) (bvad)

scrubbers._about: CO2 removal. The cabin loop is the primary; parts are backups (or the primary when they regenerate and the loop does not). failPerTrip is the chance the unit stops during the cruise (1 − reliability; estimate). mmHg: the cabin's partial pressure of CO2 while it works.

loop_open._src: apolloLioh, liohChem (canisters changed every 12 h: a sawtooth; levels: estimate from Shuttle LiOH operations)

loop_regenerative._src: cdra (ISS CDRA: 4.16 kg/day for four, about 1 kW; the ISS cabin averages about 3 mmHg)

co2_scrubber._src: camras (Orion's amine swing beds, regenerated by the vacuum of space); reliability 0.995 from the part

lioh_canisters._src: liohChem, apolloLioh (an Apollo canister weighed about 8 lb with about 4.3 lb of LiOH: 0.6 of the part is LiOH, estimate)

rigged._src: apollo13Co2 (the crew taped spare canisters into a new box; CO₂ had reached about 15 mmHg)

loop_open._src: Apollo, Dragon: water from tanks and bags

water._bufferSrc: estimate (a week of drinking water kept as a reserve with a recycler)

radiation._about: Areal density in g/cm² of aluminium-equivalent shielding: water and polyethylene count 1.3 times aluminium per g/cm² against solar protons (spe). The cruise multiplies its 1.8 mSv/day (rad) by gcrFactor; the solar storm's dose falls off with the shielding (cruise data.json).
radiation._wallSrc: spe (NASA's 'thinly shielded' crew module, ≤ 5 g/cm²; estimate for every capsule)
radiation._nookSrc: estimate: a one-person storm shelter about 1 × 1 × 1.5 m, 8 m² of wall
radiation._cabinSrc: estimate: inner wall area of a small crew cabin
radiation._atHandSrc: estimate: the food and water at hand in the cabin, about 4 g/cm² of water around a crouching crew member

radiation_shelter._src: the part (600 kg of water walls) over nookM2

cygnus_pcm._src: estimate: cargo bags and water packed round the crew

radiation._waterWallSrc: the module kit option water_wall (+150 kg of water bags on the walls)
radiation._gcrSrc: gcrShield (galactic cosmic rays: about 1 % less dose per g/cm² of water in the first tens of g/cm²; aluminium helps little. Sleeping in the shelter: a third of each day; estimate)

sources.text: NASA EMU: primary O₂ 1.2 lbm at 900 psia, secondary O₂ 2.6 lbm at 6000 psia (30 min). NASA NTRS 20230008922 (ICES 2023, EMU regulators) and NTRS 19920007771.
EMU sized for an average metabolic rate of 1000 BTU/h (293 W) over 7 h plus 30 min of reserve (NASA EMU handbook figures).
Apollo lunar EVAs: peak metabolic rates of about 1500–2000 BTU/h (440–590 W) when moving fast; running uses 1600 BTU/h (469 W), 1.6 × walking. NASA ICES-2021 metabolic paper.
Weir: each litre of O₂ the body uses releases about 20.2 kJ; 1 kg of O₂ is 699.8 L at 0 °C. So 293 W uses 0.075 kg/h and the EMU's 0.544 kg lasts 7.3 h.
NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (NASA/TP-2015-218570 Rev 2, 2022): O₂ 0.82–0.84 kg per person per day, CO₂ 1.04 kg/day, drinking water 2.5 kg/day.
ISS EVA prebreathe: 2–4 h of pure O₂ before a 29.6 kPa suit to purge nitrogen; Apollo crews lived in 5 psi oxygen and needed none.

Habitable volumes: Mercury 1.7 m³, Gemini 2.55 m³, Apollo CM 6.17 m³, Soyuz descent module 3.5 m³, Orion 8.95 m³ (316 ft³), Crew Dragon 9.3 m³, Starliner 11 m³, New Shepard 15 m³ (530 ft³), Starship about 1000 m³ (NASA, SpaceX, Boeing, Blue Origin fact sheets).
Volga inflatable airlock (Voskhod 2, 1965): about 2.5 m long and 1.0 m wide inside when inflated (1.2 m outside).
Industrial 50 L steel oxygen cylinder: about 10.4 kg of oxygen at 150 bar (14 kg at 200 bar), tare about 55–65 kg (Linde, BOC cylinder data). Valve seat leak criterion ISO 10297: 6 cm³/h.
NASA Nitrogen Oxygen Recharge System: composite-overwrapped tank holding about 36.3 kg (80 lbm) of O₂ at 41.4 MPa (6000 psi). NTRS 20110012004.
Apollo service module oxygen tank: 320 lb of supercritical O₂ at 865–935 psi, vacuum-jacketed. Apollo 13 Review Board report (1970).

ESA, Orion: Air and water: the European Service Module carries three oxygen tanks with 90 kg in all and one nitrogen tank with 30 kg, mixed into the capsule for the crew to breathe; plus 240 kg of water.
ATV Integrated Cargo Carrier: up to 100 kg of oxygen, nitrogen and air in gas tanks (ESA).
MOXIE on Perseverance made oxygen from the Martian air, up to 12 g/h (NASA/JPL 2023).
Apollo CM LiOH canisters: two in use at all times, one replaced every 12 hours (Smithsonian NASM A19980055000); a flight canister weighs about 8 lb.
2 LiOH + CO₂ → Li₂CO₃ + H₂O: 0.919 kg of CO₂ per kg of LiOH in theory; flight canisters use about three quarters of it (estimate).
Apollo 13: the lunar module's round LiOH sockets could not take the command module's square canisters; the crew built an adapter as CO₂ neared 15 mmHg.
ISS Carbon Dioxide Removal Assembly: about 450 lb, 1000 W, removes 4.16 kg of CO₂ a day for a crew of four.
CAMRAS: amine CO₂ and water sorbent in pressure-swing beds regenerated by space vacuum, baselined for Orion and flown on Artemis I (NASA NTRS).
NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2: cabin ppCO₂ at or below about 3 mmHg for long missions (headaches above that on the ISS).
ISS Environmental Control and Life Support System reached 98 % water recovery in 2023 with the Brine Processor Assembly (NASA).
MSL RAD measured 1.84 ± 0.33 mSv/day inside the spacecraft on the way to Mars (Zeitlin et al., Science 340, 2013).

Townsend, Nealy & Wilson, Preliminary Estimates of Radiation Exposures for Manned Interplanetary Missions from Anomalously Large Solar Flare Events, NASA TM-100620 (1988), NTRS 19880016043: the August 1972 event could be life-threatening behind ≤ 5 g/cm²; about 10 g/cm² of water or 13 g/cm² of aluminium keeps it under 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the blood-forming organs, so water is about 1.3 times as effective. Its blood-forming-organ dose falls about e-fold every 7–10 g/cm² of aluminium between 5 and 20 g/cm²; the game uses 8 (estimate within that range).

Galactic cosmic rays are hard to stop: Zeitlin (2013) notes even a foot of aluminium would not change the cruise dose much; hydrogen-rich shields cut it by roughly a quarter through 20–30 g/cm² (NASA HZETRN/OLTARIS studies; estimate).
NASA-STD-3001 (2022): career effective dose limit 600 mSv; 30-day blood-forming-organ limit 250 mGy-Eq.
Soyuz MS-09 (August 2018): a 2 mm hole leaking air from the ISS was found and sealed by the crew within about a day.
Air through a small hole from 101 kPa into vacuum flows choked: about 0.24 g/s per mm² (ideal), times a discharge coefficient of about 0.6.
